A1-A2.headline: Sharing Ideas And Works In The Modern World

pages.text: The free-culture movement helps people share and change creative work. It wants to make sure that art and books are easy to use. Lawrence Lessig is a famous leader in this group. He started Creative Commons to help people share their ideas with others.
pages.caption: Lawrence Lessig, a leader of the movement.

imageProvenance.credit: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA (CC BY 2.0)

pages.text: In 1998, the United States made a new law. It gave copyright owners more time to keep their work. This meant people could not use the work for many years. Many people did not like this. They thought it made it hard to be creative.

Lessig created a new system called Creative Commons. It lets creators choose how others use their work. By 2008, the group made clear rules for what is free. These rules help people know what they can change and share with the public.

This movement is like the group that makes free computer software. Some people even think piracy is okay because they do not like strict laws. They want a world where information is free for everyone to use and learn from every day.

B1-B2.headline: How The Free Culture Movement Changes Creative Works

pages.text: The free-culture movement promotes the freedom to share and change creative works. Supporters believe that sharing content helps society grow. A leader in this field founded Creative Commons to help creators share their work easily while still keeping some rights over their own creations.
pages.caption: A leader in the movement in 2005.

imageProvenance.credit: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA (CC BY 2.0)

evidence.articleCaption: Lawrence Lessig, an influential activist of the free-culture movement, in 2005

pages.text: In 1998, the U.S. Congress passed the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act. This law added twenty years to copyright protections. Critics argued that this created a culture of needing permission, which limits creativity and makes the public space for ideas smaller by keeping works private for much longer.

Creative Commons offered a new way to handle copyright. By 2008, the movement set clear rules for what counts as free content. These rules ensure that shared works can be changed and used by the public.

The movement shares ideas with open-source software groups. While most members focus on legal sharing, some support piracy because they view strict copyright as unfair. They seek a balance between protecting creators and allowing the public to access and change knowledge.

C1-C2.headline: Challenging Permission Culture Through The Free Culture Movement

pages.text: The free-culture movement advocates for the unrestricted distribution and modification of creative content, positioning itself against the restrictive nature of modern copyright. Lawrence Lessig, a central figure in this discourse, established Creative Commons to provide a framework for sharing that balances creator protection with public access.
pages.caption: Lawrence Lessig, an influential activist in 2005.

imageProvenance.credit: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James Duncan Davidson of Portland, Oregon, USA (CC BY 2.0)

evidence.articleCaption: Lawrence Lessig, an influential activist of the free-culture movement, in 2005

pages.text: The 1998 Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act serves as a focal point for the movement's criticism. By extending copyright terms by two decades, the legislation intensified concerns regarding a permission culture that stifles innovation and limits the expansion of the public domain for future creators.

Lessig's initiative evolved into a robust licensing system, eventually leading to the 2008 Definition of Free Cultural Works. This collaborative effort established rigorous standards for freedom, ensuring that content labeled as 'free' remains accessible for modification and reuse, thereby fostering a more vibrant, remix-oriented cultural landscape.

Rooted in the ethos of the free software movement, the free-culture movement extends these principles to all creative domains. While some adherents go as far as supporting piracy as a form of protest against perceived illegitimate monopolies, the core mission remains the democratization of knowledge and the promotion of cultural progress.
